title: Moving Zombiehood out of event sheets
description: How I’m moving a shipped Construct game into JavaScript and TypeScript without changing how it plays.
paragraphs: Zombiehood was built in Construct, where a lot of the game’s logic lived in visual event sheets. That was a good way to get the game made and shipped. Over time, though, thousands of interconnected conditions and actions made some systems harder to understand, test, and change with confidence.

I’m now moving that logic into a JavaScript and TypeScript codebase. This is not a rewrite where the old game gets thrown away and rebuilt behind closed doors. It is a progressive migration: move one behavior, prove that the game still behaves the same way, then remove the event logic it replaces.

sections.heading: Why migrate a game that already shipped?
paragraphs: Event sheets are fast and expressive, especially when a project is young. Zombiehood did not stay young. Inventory, equipment, enemies, menus, saves, procedural systems, and platform behavior accumulated across 46 event-sheet files. A change in one place could depend on instance selection or event ordering somewhere else.

Typed code gives those systems names and boundaries. It gives me smaller files, searchable call sites, explicit inputs, reusable helpers, and tests that can run without clicking through the editor. The goal is not to replace Construct as the engine. The goal is to make the game logic easier to own.

sections.heading: The process
paragraphs: I work in slices that are small enough to review but complete enough to mean something. First I inventory the native behavior: what gets selected, which values change, what happens immediately, and what waits until another tick. Then I write a typed equivalent and run it against the same cases.

Construct still owns the parts that genuinely belong to the engine or have not moved yet. A thin event facade can select an object or create an instance, then hand control to TypeScript. Once the new owner is proven, I remove the replaced conditions and actions from the event sheet and record the before-and-after counts.
That boundary moves a little at a time. It lets the shipped game remain the reference instead of asking a new implementation to reproduce years of behavior from memory.

sections.heading: A deeper dive: preserving equipment cooldowns
paragraphs: A recent slice moved the equipment inventory lifecycle: picking up an item, replacing the current slot, loading its catalog data, updating the HUD, dropping the old item, and carrying its remaining cooldown into the world.

The cooldown is a small detail with a large gameplay consequence. If a player can drop and pick up equipment to reset a timer, the migration has changed the rules. The typed implementation keeps the existing timer tags and transfers the remaining time in either direction.

sections.heading: How I measure progress
paragraphs: The numbers above come from a repository tool that reads named Git commits, not from a hand-maintained checklist. It counts the same event node types in every snapshot and separately measures authored TypeScript. That makes the comparison repeatable as the migration continues.

The numbers are useful, but they are not a percent-complete bar. One event block can hide a lot of behavior, while a larger group may be straightforward. More TypeScript lines do not automatically mean better code. The useful claim is narrower: between these two commits, the project contains 1,019 fewer counted event blocks and the migrated behaviors have explicit code and test coverage.

sections.heading: Testing the handoff
paragraphs: Each slice gets pure tests where the logic allows it, project and JSON validation, and focused runtime checks in an instrumented Construct preview. The equipment checkpoint also ran the broader migration regression before it was recorded.

Those checks do not make every risk disappear. Historical saves, normal unsuppressed gameplay, physical devices, and interactions outside a focused fixture still need deliberate playtesting. The migration ledger records those limits so a green test is not mistaken for proof of the entire game.

sections.heading: Where it stands
paragraphs: This is still active work. The latest snapshot in this draft has 3,474 counted event blocks across the same 46 sheets. Some sheets are mixed: TypeScript owns a complete behavior while Construct still handles an engine boundary or another system nearby.

Before publishing the final version, I want to add one visual before-and-after from an event sheet, a diagram of the Construct-to-TypeScript boundary, and refreshed numbers from a stable checkpoint. The important story is already clear: Zombiehood is becoming easier to reason about without asking players to absorb the cost of a wholesale rewrite.
